newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: FOCUS - Swiss merger to create global group.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Swiss merger to create global group.

text.p: Two of Switzerland's top financial groups, Credit Suisse Group and Winterthur Group, on Monday announced plans to merge and create one of the world's leading financial service providers.

The merger catapults Credit Suisse Group into the position of undisputed leader among Switzerland's Big Three Banks and takes place amidst deep structural changes in global financial markets and fierce competition in the insurance industry.
"The merger is a powerful, forward-looking response to developments in the financial services market," said Lukas Muehlemann, chief executive of the combined group.

The stock market reacted positively to the planned merger and analysts were also in favour of the move, noting it is likely to put pressure on Union Bank of Switzerland UBS and Swiss Bank Corp SBC to meet the challenge.
"I think this puts pressure on the other big Swiss banks," said Thomas Della Putta of private bankers Pictet & Cie.

After initially jumping almost four percent in pre-bourse euphoria, both shares eased but were still firmer. Shares of Winterthur were up one percent at 1,532 francs in mid-morning and shares of Credit Suisse were up 0.8 percent at 210 francs.
The merger comes after months of intense speculation about Winterthur and only days after financier Martin Ebner said he wanted to acquire a majority of the insurer.
One analyst questioned whether the timing of the merger was dictated by the stake amassed in Winterthur by Ebner's BZ Group.

The combination of Credit Suisse, currently Switzerland's second largest bank, with Winterthur, the third largest insurer, should result in synergies of 300 to 350 million Swiss francs within three years from higher income and cost-cutting.
A maximum of 500 jobs worldwide will be lost, but the two companies said in a joint statement there would be no layoffs.

"The two companies are now in an even better position to provide their personal and corporate customers with attractive financial products combining the advantages of banking and insurance solutions," the companies said.

Shareholders of both companies will be asked to approve the deal on September 5. Assuming approval, Credit Suisse Group will offer Winterthur shareholders to swap one of their shares for 7.3 Credit Suisse shares.

Winterthur will then become part of the Credit Suisse Group, boosting its total assets to around 700 billion francs, giving it a market capitalisation of more than 50 billion and around 700 billion francs in assets under management.
The merger illustrates the blurring distinction between banks and insurance companies where market position and market presence is becoming increasingly critical.

"Strategically, this makes sense for Credit Suisse. The general trend in Europe clearly goes towards bancassurance. It's not the insurance companies that need the banks, it's the banks that need the insurance companies to be more competetive," said Della Putta.

Credit Suisse Group and Winterthur entered into a strategic alliance in 1996 to explore joint sales opportunities and "it became clear that there would be additional potential in strengthening ties further," the companies said.
"The merger will allow the group to exploit to the full the advantages of being a banassurance provider in all customer and market segments," they added.
The deal was announced only a few days after investment group BZ Trust on Saturday said its aim was to acquire a majority in Winterthur.
Ebner's BZ group and its customers currently hold roughly 30 percent of Winterthur and have been actively buying the shares for months, pushing up its price.

"A new situation arose with the large stake taken by (BZ Group's Martin) Ebner. This appears to have forced CS and Winterthur to act. The situation was becoming too threatening in the sense that Ebner could have given control of Winterthur to an outsider or sought to take power himself," said analyst Christoph Bieri of Zurich Kantonalbank.
Ebner is Switzerland's most controversial professional investor after a drawn-out fight with management at UBS over how to raise the bank's profitability.
